Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

parliament noun

also Parliament, legislature, national assembly, congress, member of parliament, MP

medieval

Traupman 356
M-O s.v. legislature, parliament

parlāmentum, parlāmentī n.

noun, second declension

a parliament

The medieval word for an assembly, from Old French parlement; Milton’s for the Parliament of the English Commonwealth, and Traupman’s for a parliament today. A member of parliament is parlāmentārius (Traupman 356) or populī lēgātus (Levi–Bini p. 21); a chamber of parliament, camera (M-O).

Other words

  • comitia, comitiōrum n. pl. — the assemblies of the Roman people

    noun, second declension, plural · also used · classical · Cic. Leg. 3.44 (Lewis & Short)

    Rome had no parliament. The people voted laws in these assemblies, on a magistrate’s proposal, and elected the magistrates there, while the senate only advised (see senate). A parliament is an elected assembly of representatives that makes the laws itself.

  • senātus, senātūs m. — a parliament (Neo-Latin); classically the senate

    noun, fourth declension · also used · modern · M-O s.v. legislature, parliament

    Milton and Tursellinus call the English Parliament and the Paris parlement senātus (Morgan–Owens).

  • lēgātī populārēs — the elected deputies; the lower house

    noun phrase, plural: lēgātus with the adjective populāris · also used · modern · Levi–Bini p. 46

    Levi and Bini’s phrase for a chamber of deputies; for a senate whose members sit for life they keep senātus.

Examples

  • Parlāmentum Reī Pūblicae Angliae

    the Parliament of the Commonwealth of EnglandMilton (1674), in M-O s.v. legislature, parliament

  • parlāmentārius (parlāmentāria)

    a member of parliamentTraupman 356
